clinicalPearls: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A, leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation; cardiac involvement is a leading cause of death and may be the only manifestation in later-onset cardiac variants.

It is an important mimic of sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and should be considered in any unexplained concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, particularly with a suggestive family history or extracardiac features.
Females, as heterozygotes, are not merely carriers and can develop significant and even severe cardiomyopathy owing to X-inactivation, so a family history following an X-linked pattern is a clue.

A characteristically low or low-normal T1 on cardiac magnetic resonance reflects sphingolipid storage and is a valuable discriminator from other causes of hypertrophy, which typically show normal or high native T1.
Late gadolinium enhancement classically involves the basal inferolateral wall and signals regional fibrosis that predicts arrhythmia and limited response to enzyme therapy.
Extracardiac clues include acroparaesthesiae, angiokeratomata, hypohidrosis, cornea verticillata, proteinuric renal disease and early stroke.

Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity in males and on GLA gene analysis in females, in whom enzyme activity may be normal; plasma lyso-Gb3 supports the diagnosis and monitoring.

Enzyme replacement therapy and oral chaperone therapy (for amenable GLA mutations) can stabilise or reduce left ventricular mass, with greatest benefit when started before extensive fibrosis develops.
reference.pathophysiology: Deficient lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A activity impairs catabolism of glycosphingolipids, leading to progressive intracellular accumulation of globotriaosylceramide within cardiomyocytes, conduction tissue, valvular tissue, vascular endothelium and smooth muscle. Storage itself accounts for only a fraction of the increased ventricular mass; the accumulated substrate triggers secondary processes of cellular hypertrophy, energetic impairment, inflammation and progressive replacement fibrosis, classically in the basal inferolateral wall. The result is concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction and, later, systolic impairment. Involvement of the conduction system and small-vessel coronary dysfunction produce conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias and angina despite unobstructed epicardial coronary arteries.
additionalDifferentials: glycogen storage cardiomyopathy (e.g. PRKAG2, Danon disease)
additionalInvestigations: alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity (definitive in males)
plasma or dried blood spot lyso-Gb3
cardiac magnetic resonance with native T1 mapping and late gadolinium enhancement
echocardiography with strain imaging for concentric hypertrophy
12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for conduction disease and arrhythmia
urinalysis and renal function for associated nephropathy
redFlags: syncope or documented sustained ventricular arrhythmia
progressive heart failure with declining systolic function
advancing conduction disease or high-grade atrioventricular block
extensive basal inferolateral late gadolinium enhancement
concurrent rapidly progressive renal impairment or stroke
reference.prognosis: Cardiac involvement is a principal determinant of survival; disease-modifying therapy started before significant fibrosis can stabilise or regress hypertrophy and improve outlook, whereas advanced fibrosis, heart failure and malignant arrhythmia carry a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: misdiagnosing Fabry cardiomyopathy as sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and missing a treatable cause
excluding disease in a symptomatic female on the basis of normal enzyme activity, when GLA testing is required
overlooking extracardiac features that would prompt earlier diagnosis
starting enzyme therapy after extensive fibrosis, when benefit is limited
attributing angina to epicardial coronary disease and missing microvascular dysfunction
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
Expert consensus recommendations on the diagnosis and management of Fabry disease
management: Disease-specific enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant alpha-galactosidase A (agalsidase alfa or beta), ideally started before significant replacement fibrosis develops
Oral pharmacological chaperone therapy (migalastat) for patients with amenable GLA missense mutations

Standard heart-failure therapy for diastolic and later systolic dysfunction, using renin-angiotensin blockade and other guideline-directed agents, with caution over rate-limiting drugs given conduction disease

Manage arrhythmia and conduction disease: pacing for atrioventricular block or bradyarrhythmia and an implantable defibrillator where arrhythmic risk is high, with anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation
Treat extracardiac disease: renin-angiotensin blockade for proteinuric nephropathy, neuropathic-pain control and stroke prevention
Surveillance with serial cardiac MRI (native T1 mapping and late gadolinium enhancement), echocardiography, ECG/ambulatory monitoring and plasma lyso-Gb3
Genetic counselling with cascade family screening for this X-linked disorder, managed within an inherited-metabolic-disease multidisciplinary team
